title: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
summary: File Deletion is the cleanup half of an intrusion: once a payload, script, or tool has done its work, the attacker removes it so that responders cannot recover the binary, read its strings, or trace where it came from. The behaviour is deliberately mundane, because every operating system already ships the verbs needed to do it, from the Windows del and erase commands through rm and unlink on Linux and macOS to rm on an ESXi host, and specialist wipers such as secure-delete utilities simply overwrite the file contents before unlinking so that recovery tools find nothing useful. Defensively, the artefact is less the missing file than the record around it. Object access auditing, endpoint process telemetry, execution history, browser or application logs, security tooling quarantine records, and backup or versioning copies may all still describe a file that no longer exists on disk, and a shell process that runs a deletion command shortly after a download or an unusual child process is far more informative than the absence of the file itself. The hard part is separating hostile cleanup from ordinary housekeeping, because installers, patch tools, temporary folders, scripted jobs, and users clear files constantly. Context is what decides it: the deleted name appearing in earlier process, share, or download telemetry, deletion of a tool rather than a document, a burst of deletions in a temporary directory immediately after execution, and recovery of the name from the Master File Table, USN change journal, or a central log pipeline that already ingested the event before the file vanished.

beginner.definition: File deletion means an attacker removes the files their attack created. They delete their own tools, scripts, and malware after they finish using them. The aim is to leave fewer traces for defenders to find.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every file an attacker copies onto your computer is evidence. It can show what they did and which tools they used. When they delete those files, that evidence can disappear. Good logging often remembers the file even after the file itself is gone. This is why logs matter so much.
howItWorks: An attacker copies a tool or part of their malware onto a computer they control in your network.
Later, during the attack or after it, they decide to remove that file to hide what happened.
They use commands that already exist on the system, such as del on Windows or rm on Linux.
On Windows the del command marks a file for removal, and the space is reused later.
Some attackers use wiping tools that overwrite the file first, so recovery software finds nothing useful.
Third-party cleanup scripts or the malware itself can delete files without any command typed by a person.
beginner.example: Think of a library. A visitor secretly borrows an old book from a shelf. Before leaving, they also remove the index card that proves the book was ever there. The shelf looks normal and the catalogue looks normal too. However, the librarian's daily log still shows that someone asked for that book that morning.
takeaways: Deleting a file is normal behaviour, so the deletion command alone does not prove an attack.
What matters is context, such as a file being deleted right after it was downloaded or run.
Collect logs to a central place quickly, because they survive even when the file does not.

objectives: Explain what file deletion is and why attackers use it after an intrusion.
Describe how built-in commands on Windows, Linux, and ESXi remove files.
Identify which log sources still record a file after it has been deleted.
Distinguish hostile cleanup from ordinary system and user housekeeping.
Summarise how file recovery artefacts such as the Master File Table help an investigation.
